headline: A rough day across the board — PLS.AX slumped nearly 6%, GXAI dropped 3%, and GOOG shed almost 3% last night, while Middle East tensions escalate with Houthis striking Riyadh and the Strait of Hormuz nearly paralysed.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara shed nearly 6% today, closing at $2.56 — its lowest level in a long time. Lithium prices remain depressed globally, and there's no near-term catalyst to turn things around. Fellow lithium miner Liontown also hit a 52-week low today, suggesting sector-wide pain rather than a Pilbara-specific issue.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI dropped 3% today following a rough night for US tech — the NASDAQ fell 1.83% last night, dragging AI-exposed stocks down with it. The ETF holds a basket of AI companies, so when big US tech names like GOOG and MSFT slide, GXAI follows.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google fell nearly 3% last night in a broad tech sell-off that hit the NASDAQ hard. There's also some competitive noise — a report noted Google Cloud is outpacing Microsoft and AWS on AI and cloud revenue, but the market seemed focused on broader risk-off sentiment rather than rewarding that news.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE slipped 1.38% today, weighed down by global risk-off sentiment and ongoing Middle East tensions that are rattling emerging market confidence. The Strait of Hormuz disruption and rising oil prices add uncertainty to many emerging economies.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft fell 1.69% last night despite recent solid earnings — the decline was part of a broader tech sector sell-off. MSFT is still up over 10% from your cost base, so this is a single bad night in an otherwise healthy position.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS eased 0.76% today, tracking the slight weakness in US markets from last night's session. The fund covers the entire US share market, so it moves with the broader US tide — nothing stock-specific here.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG slipped a modest 0.6% today, reflecting mild softness across both Aussie and international shares. As a diversified multi-asset fund, it cushioned the broader tech weakness well — this is normal daily noise.

movers.name: DHHF
movers.note: DHHF dipped 0.63% today in line with broad market softness. As a 100% global shares ETF, it mirrored the gentle pullback across world markets. No specific catalyst — just a quiet down day.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two was the standout last night, rising 2.44% to $225.78 — the only green holding in the portfolio. News that Rockstar (Take-Two's studio) actively shut down an unauthorised GTA 6 PC port and a fan-made GTA 5 iPhone port reinforced that the GTA 6 IP is closely guarded, keeping hype alive ahead of the game's release.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Lithium pain continues — hold your nerve
watch_today.detail: Pilbara dropped nearly 6% today and is now down 62% from your cost base. This stings, but the story hasn't fundamentally changed — lithium is in a prolonged price trough and the whole sector is hurting (Liontown also hit a 52-week low today). Selling now locks in the loss. For a long-term holder, the thesis is that lithium demand for EVs and batteries will recover. Sit tight unless your conviction in that story has changed.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI ETF dragged by tech sell-off — hold
watch_today.detail: GXAI fell 3% today, tracking the NASDAQ's rough night. It's now down 22% from your cost base, which is uncomfortable. But Google just launched Gemini 4 Neon claiming it beats GPT-6.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 on most benchmarks — the AI race is as alive as ever. The long-term case for AI infrastructure spending remains intact. No reason to sell; this is volatility in a growth theme.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Down nearly 3% last night — still hold
watch_today.detail: Google fell 2.91% last night in a broad tech sell-off. The stock is down 12.65% from your cost base. There's no structural bad news — Google Cloud is reportedly outpacing Microsoft and AWS on AI and cloud revenue growth, and the core ad business remains dominant. This looks like market noise rather than a thesis break. Hold.

watch_today.title: TTWO: Only winner in the portfolio last night — hold on
watch_today.detail: Take-Two rose 2.44% last night and is now 4.6% up from your cost base. The GTA franchise IP is being actively protected (Rockstar shut down two unauthorised ports this week), keeping excitement building ahead of GTA 6. Nothing to do here — just enjoy the green day and hold for the long run.

watch_today.title: Middle East escalation pushing oil higher — watch energy costs
watch_today.detail: Crude oil jumped nearly 2% last night to US$83.62 a barrel. The Strait of Hormuz — one of the world's most critical oil shipping lanes — is reportedly 'virtually paralysed' with 400 ships waiting, following Houthi attacks and Iranian pressure. If this continues, higher petrol prices could feed into Australian inflation, which is already running hot at 4.9%.

watch_today.title: Australian inflation hits 4.9% — RBA rate decision looms
watch_today.detail: New inflation data out today showed Australia's CPI jumped to 4.9%, driven largely by fuel price surges. Treasurer Chalmers rejected recession fears but acknowledged a 'very serious moment' for the economy. The RBA has signalled rates remain restrictive — a rate cut looks unlikely anytime soon, which keeps pressure on mortgage holders and consumer spending.

world.summary: The Middle East conflict dominated global headlines today, with the Strait of Hormuz nearly paralysed and Houthi forces striking a skyscraper in Riyadh. Separately, California is bracing for record-breaking tidal flooding.

stories.title: Strait of Hormuz nearly paralysed as Houthis strike Riyadh skyscraper
stories.source: Il Sole 24 ORE / The New York Times
stories.why_it_matters: Yemen's Houthi rebels launched a missile strike on a skyscraper in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, wounding 11 people — a dramatic escalation that takes the conflict directly into a major city. At the same time, Iran has essentially choked the Strait of Hormuz, with roughly 400 ships sitting idle waiting to pass. The Strait carries about 20% of the world's traded oil, so any prolonged blockage sends oil prices sharply higher — which showed up last night with crude jumping nearly 2% to US$83.62. Higher oil means higher petrol prices at the bowser for everyday Australians, and more fuel to Australia's already-hot inflation.

stories.title: Dubai and Middle East flight disruption continues as Saudi Arabia confirms another attack
stories.why_it_matters: Flight cancellations and route suspensions across the Middle East are continuing to pile up as the conflict spreads. Dubai — a major international transit hub for Australians travelling to Europe — is seeing significant disruption. Saudi Arabia has confirmed multiple new attacks on its territory. If you have travel through the region planned in coming weeks, it's worth checking your itinerary and airline communications.

stories.title: How the Iran war is reshaping the US military presence in the Middle East
stories.why_it_matters: The conflict is forcing the United States to significantly rethink how it deploys its military forces across the Middle East. With Iranian-backed groups engaging on multiple fronts — from Houthi attacks in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, to pressure on the Strait of Hormuz — the US is repositioning assets in the region. This is a major geopolitical shift that could affect global trade routes, energy supply, and Western foreign policy commitments for years.

stories.title: California beaches close as record-breaking tides and major flooding loom
stories.why_it_matters: Beaches up and down the California coast have been closed as the state prepares for record-breaking high tides and severe flooding. This is the latest in a string of extreme weather events battering the US west coast, and scientists are linking the intensity to long-term climate patterns. For Australian investors, California is a major centre of US economic activity — particularly tech — so sustained climate disruption there has real economic ripple effects.

stories.title: Fidelity releases 2027 economic and market outlook
stories.why_it_matters: Fidelity, one of the world's largest investment managers, has published its 2027 market outlook — a useful reference point as we head into the final months of 2026. While specific details weren't included in the article text, major institutional outlooks like this tend to shape sentiment and fund flows in the new year. Worth keeping an eye out for the full report if you're thinking about portfolio positioning heading into 2027.

markets.summary: It was a rough night in the US last night — the NASDAQ dropped 1.83% and the S&P 500 fell 1%, dragging most of the portfolio with it. Closer to home, the ASX closed down a modest 0.39% today. Oil jumped on Middle East tensions, while gold eased slightly and the Aussie dollar was barely changed.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Soft close today, down 0.39% — the inflation print and global jitters weighed on sentiment.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session saw a 1% fall — broad risk-off selling across Wall Street.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Tech took the brunt of it last night, with the NASDAQ dropping 1.83%.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil jumped nearly 2% last night as the Strait of Hormuz disruption rattled supply expectations.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold slipped slightly last night — still near historically elevated levels.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar was essentially unchanged — sitting at 66.3 US cents.

politics.summary: Australia's economy is under real pressure today — fresh inflation data came in at 4.9%, driven by surging fuel costs, sparking a heated political debate about whether the RBA should hold rates or whether Chalmers needs to act. The Treasurer is walking a tightrope between recession fears and runaway prices.

stories.title: Inflation jumps to 4.9% as fuel prices surge
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's latest inflation figure came in at 4.9%, well above where the Reserve Bank wants it. The main culprit is surging fuel prices — not entirely within the RBA's control, since it's largely driven by the Middle East conflict and oil supply disruption. Some economists argue the RBA should hold rates steady rather than hike further, since rate rises don't fix supply-side oil shocks but do hurt mortgage holders. For everyday Australians, this means the cost of living squeeze is not letting up.

stories.title: Treasurer Chalmers rejects recession fears but warns of 'very serious moment'
stories.why_it_matters: Treasurer Jim Chalmers pushed back on growing recession fears today, but acknowledged the economy is at a 'very serious moment'. With inflation at 4.9% and interest rates already biting, there's real tension in Canberra about what to do next. Chalmers also flagged a major budget update with spending cuts coming — suggesting the government is bracing for a deteriorating fiscal position. The balance between cutting spending (which could tip into recession) and spending to support growth is incredibly difficult right now.

stories.title: Chalmers flags major budget update and spending cuts
stories.why_it_matters: The Treasurer has signalled a major mid-year budget update is coming, with spending cuts on the table. This comes as Australia faces a tricky combination of high inflation, high interest rates, and slowing economic growth. Cuts to government spending could free up fiscal headroom but risk tipping the economy into a slowdown. Households that rely on government support payments or public services could feel the pinch directly.

stories.title: RBA speech: Rates remain restrictive amid economic cross-currents
stories.why_it_matters: The RBA delivered a speech overnight confirming that interest rates are still in 'restrictive' territory — meaning they're deliberately set high enough to slow the economy and cool inflation. The phrase 'cross-currents' signals the RBA is aware of competing forces: high inflation on one hand, rising recession risk on the other. In plain English: don't expect a rate cut soon, and don't expect a hike either — the RBA is watching and waiting.

stories.title: Australia's Digital Duty of Care bill nears law — free speech concerns raised
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's new Digital Duty of Care legislation — which would force big tech platforms to protect users from harmful content — is moving closer to becoming law. Critics are raising concerns about free speech impacts, arguing the rules are too broad and could lead to over-censorship of legitimate content. For social media users and tech companies operating in Australia, this could mean significant changes to what gets moderated and how platforms are held accountable.

ai.summary: Big AI news today: Google launched Gemini 4 Neon claiming it beats rivals on most benchmarks, while OpenAI and Anthropic staff are reportedly worried some of their own unreleased models are too risky to release. Australia also made global headlines with world-first criminal penalties for AI misuse.

stories.title: Google unveils Gemini 4 Neon — claims it beats GPT-6.2 and Claude Opus 5.5
stories.why_it_matters: Google dropped its latest flagship AI model — Gemini 4 Neon — and is claiming it outperforms OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 on most benchmarks. If true, this is a significant moment in the AI race: Google has been playing catch-up to OpenAI's ChatGPT for a couple of years, and a genuine lead on the most capable models would be a big deal for Alphabet's cloud and consumer products. Worth watching how independent testers rate it over coming days.

stories.title: OpenAI and Anthropic staff fear some unreleased models are too dangerous to ship
stories.why_it_matters: Reports are emerging that employees inside both OpenAI and Anthropic — the two leading AI labs — are privately worried that some of their next-generation models are too risky to release to the public. This is significant because it comes from insiders, not critics. The concern is likely around models that are becoming harder to control or that could be misused for serious harm. It raises real questions about the pace of AI development and whether the race to outcompete is overriding safety considerations.

stories.title: Australia introduces world-first criminal penalties for AI misuse
stories.why_it_matters: Australia has become the first country in the world to introduce criminal penalties specifically for AI misuse — meaning individuals or companies could face criminal charges (not just fines) for using AI in harmful ways. The new laws create an interesting accountability puzzle: if an AI system makes a harmful decision, who goes to jail — the developer, the company using it, or the person who deployed it? The specifics are still being worked through, but it marks a dramatic shift in how governments are approaching AI regulation.

stories.title: The AI hardware loop threatening Nvidia's dominance
stories.why_it_matters: A new analysis argues that a structural shift is underway that could eventually undercut Nvidia's near-monopoly on AI chips. The 'hardware loop' refers to the cycle where AI labs build custom chips for their own models, reducing their need to buy from Nvidia. Companies like Google (with its TPUs), Amazon, and Meta are all developing in-house AI silicon. If this trend accelerates, Nvidia faces real long-term competition — relevant to anyone holding AI-focused investments like GXAI.

stories.title: Google Cloud outpaces Microsoft and AWS on AI and cloud revenue
stories.why_it_matters: According to Cloud Wars analysis, Google Cloud has pulled ahead of both Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services (AWS) in AI and cloud revenue growth. This is a meaningful reversal — Microsoft has dominated cloud AI headlines with its OpenAI partnership, while Google was seen as playing catch-up. If Google Cloud is genuinely accelerating, it's a positive signal for Alphabet's (GOOG) long-term earnings trajectory and validates the investment thesis for holding the stock through the current dip.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final delivered a thriller, Jannik Sinner is facing a potentially season-ending knee surgery, Cameron Munster has set the NRL free agency market on fire, and the AFL handed out its MVP awards.

stories.title: Roosters defeat Knights 19-18 in NRL Grand Final thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters won the 2026 NRL premiership by the narrowest possible margin, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 at Accor Stadium on Sunday. One point in a Grand Final — doesn't get more nerve-wracking than that. It's the Roosters' latest title in what has been a dynasty built on consistent roster management and big-game experience.

stories.title: Jannik Sinner faces Australian Open absence after knee surgery
stories.why_it_matters: World number one Jannik Sinner has undergone what his camp is calling 'minor surgery' on his right knee, casting serious doubt over his appearance at the Australian Open in January. Sinner won the Australian Open title earlier this year (his second consecutive), making him the overwhelming favourite heading in. If he can't defend, it blows the men's draw wide open — good news for Aussie fans who might see a local challenger go deeper.

stories.title: Cameron Munster rejects offer, sends NRL market into frenzy
stories.why_it_matters: Cameron Munster — one of the NRL's biggest stars — has knocked back a contract offer, sending clubs scrambling and the rumour mill into overdrive. Munster's destination is now one of the biggest storylines heading into the 2027 season. With the PNG Chiefs emerging as a well-funded expansion side that's already signing big names (including England's AJ Brimson on a three-year deal), Munster's next move could genuinely reshape the competition's balance of power.

stories.title: PNG Chiefs spending big — are they blowing their money?
stories.why_it_matters: The Herald is crunching the numbers on the PNG Chiefs' recruitment blitz ahead of their NRL debut. The expansion club is spending aggressively, confirming AJ Brimson (England international) on a three-year deal and chasing multiple big-name signings. The question the article poses is whether this spending spree is strategic roster-building or reckless. For NRL fans, a well-resourced PNG side could be one of the most exciting new additions to the competition in years.

stories.title: AFL MVP Awards: Geelong star takes top honour, Melbourne dominate
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL MVP awards were handed out this week, with a Geelong Cats star capping a stellar season by taking the top individual honour. Melbourne (the Demons) dominated the team awards, suggesting they remain one of the competition's elite sides heading into the off-season. No article text with specific player names was available, so check afl.com.au for the full list of winners.
